Executive Summary

Over the 26-year period from January 3, 2000 to January 29, 2026, Nike Inc. (NKE) delivered a cumulative return of +1,282%, transforming every $1,000 invested into approximately $13,820. This translates to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.60%, comfortably outpacing the long-run average return of the S&P 500.

However, the path was far from smooth. Nike’s stock exhibited an annualized volatility of 31.2% and endured a maximum drawdown of −68.5% from its November 2021 all-time high of $166.25 to $52.31 in April 2025 — the deepest trough in the dataset. This underscores that even among elite compounders, investors must be prepared for multi-year periods of severe capital impairment.

The stock’s journey divides into three distinct macro-phases: a steady recovery and growth era (2000–2009) following the dot-com and early-2000s downturn, a spectacular bull run (2010–2021) driven by DTC transformation and global brand power, and a sharp retracement (2022–2026) that erased over two-thirds of the peak valuation. At $61.81, the stock ended January 2026 near levels last seen in early 2018.

Long-Term Price Trend Analysis

The chart below presents Nike’s full price history with 50-day and 200-day simple moving averages, shaded regions for notable crisis periods, and markers for the all-time high and low.

Figure 1: NKE daily adjusted closing price with 50-day and 200-day SMAs. Shaded areas indicate crisis / bear-market periods.
Figure 2: Log-scale view reveals the compounding growth rate and the magnitude of the post-2021 decline relative to the long-term trend.

Phase 1 — Base Formation & Recovery (2000–2003): Nike’s adjusted close began at $4.47 in January 2000, immediately fell to its all-time low of $2.47 by February 2000 (a −45% decline in under two months driven by earnings disappointments and broader dot-com contagion), then spent roughly three years building a base before breaking out above $6 in late 2003 (+49.3% for the year).

Phase 2 — Steady Appreciation (2004–2007): Nike posted consistent gains, rising from ~$6.50 to ~$12.60. The stock gained +34.9% in 2004 and +33.1% in 2007, establishing a pattern of steady mid-teens to mid-thirties annual returns. The 200-day SMA trended upward nearly uninterrupted.

Phase 3 — Global Financial Crisis (2008–2009): The GFC clipped Nike by −18.1% in 2008, but this was a relatively mild drawdown compared to the broader market. The recovery was swift: +26.9% in 2009, with the stock closing above its pre-crisis high by late that year. This resilience was an early signal of Nike’s defensive quality characteristics.

Phase 4 — The Great Bull Run (2010–2021): This twelve-year stretch was extraordinary. Nike rose from $13.27 to an all-time high of $166.25 in November 2021 — a ~12.5x appreciation. Key catalysts included consistent revenue growth, margin expansion via the direct-to-consumer pivot, international expansion (particularly China), and multiple expansion as the market rewarded Nike’s premium brand positioning. Standout years included 2013 (+53.8%), 2019 (+38.2%), and 2020 (+39.7%). The COVID-19 crash in March 2020 caused a brief −36% intraday decline but was fully recovered within months, fueled by e-commerce acceleration.

Phase 5 — Post-Peak Decline (2022–2026): From the November 2021 peak at $166.25, the stock entered a persistent downtrend. The decline accelerated through multiple catalysts: inventory overhang in 2022 (−28.2%), competitive headwinds and China uncertainty in 2023 (−7.4%), and strategic missteps in 2024 (−27.8%). By April 2025, the stock touched $52.31 — a −68.5% drawdown from peak, the deepest in the dataset. At $61.81 as of late January 2026, recovery remains tentative.

Key Observation: The −68.5% maximum drawdown (Nov 2021 to Apr 2025) is the most severe decline in the dataset, surpassing even the early-2000 crash. At 3.4 years in duration, it also represents the longest sustained decline, testing the conviction of long-term holders.

Volatility and Risk Assessment

Volatility is the price of admission for equity returns. Nike’s annualized volatility of 31.2% — calculated from daily log returns over 6,559 trading days — positions it as moderately volatile for a large-cap consumer brand. The chart below shows how this risk materialized as drawdowns from peak value.

Figure 3: Drawdown from prior peak. The post-2021 drawdown of −68.5% dwarfs all prior episodes.
Figure 4: 30-day rolling annualized volatility. Peaks align with the 2008 GFC (~95%) and COVID-19 crash (~92%).
Figure 5: 60-day rolling average of daily price range as a percentage of closing price — a proxy for intraday volatility.
Figure 6: Distribution of daily returns. The distribution exhibits mild negative skew and fat tails typical of equity returns.

Major Drawdown Episodes

  • Feb 2000: −45% in 7 weeks (earnings miss + dot-com)
  • 2008 GFC: −40% peak-to-trough; recovered by mid-2009
  • COVID-19 (Mar 2020): ~−36% intraday; full recovery in 5 months
  • Nov 2021 – Apr 2025: −68.5% over 3.4 years — the deepest and longest

Volatility Regime Analysis

  • Highest 30d vol: ~95% annualized (Nov 2008, GFC)
  • Second highest: ~92% annualized (Apr 2020, COVID)
  • Typical calm regime: 15–25% annualized
  • Daily range in crises: 5–8% vs normal 1.5–2.5%

The volatility time series reveals distinct regimes. The 2000s were structurally more volatile than the 2010s, likely reflecting Nike’s smaller market cap and less institutional ownership in the earlier period. The 2020s have seen volatility re-elevate, driven by both the COVID shock and the sustained post-2021 decline.

Trading Volume Patterns

Volume tells us how much conviction accompanied price movements. The chart below overlays price and monthly average volume, with green/red bars indicating months with net positive/negative returns.

Figure 7: NKE price (top) and monthly average volume (bottom). Green = net positive month, Red = net negative month.

Secular volume decline (2000s → 2010s): Average daily volume fell from ~12.5M shares in the 2000s to ~9.0M in the 2010s, even as the stock price rose dramatically. This likely reflects the shift toward institutional buy-and-hold strategies, ETF inclusion, and reduced speculative turnover as Nike became a widely-held blue chip.

Volume resurgence (2024–2026): Average daily volume surged to ~11.6M in 2024 and ~16.7M in 2025 — the highest levels since the mid-2000s. This aligns with the accelerating price decline, suggesting institutional portfolio rebalancing and active selling pressure.

Decade contrast: The 2010s were remarkably consistent — only 2016 posted a loss (−16.4%), and the decade delivered a CAGR of 21.6%. The 2020s have been the mirror image, with four consecutive negative years from 2022–2025 eroding what was built in 2020–2021.

Best single year: 2013 at +53.8%, driven by strong DTC momentum and margin expansion. Worst single year: 2022 at −28.2%, as inventory bloat and post-COVID demand normalization pressured the stock. The −27.8% decline in 2024 was nearly as severe, marking back-to-back >25% annual losses for the first time in the dataset.

Key Takeaways and Investment Implications

The Bull Case

  • Proven compounder: 10.6% CAGR over 26 years, turning $1K into ~$13.8K
  • Resilience in downturns: Prior to 2022, Nike consistently recovered from drawdowns faster than the broad market
  • Brand durability: Through multiple macro crises, the business franchise remained intact
  • Current valuation: Stock is at levels last seen in 2018, potentially offering value if earnings stabilize

The Bear Case

  • Unprecedented drawdown: −68.5% peak-to-trough suggests structural issues, not just cyclical weakness
  • Four consecutive losing years: 2022–2025 is the worst sustained performance in the dataset
  • Elevated volatility: Volume and vol are rising in the decline, suggesting forced selling, not orderly correction
  • Broken trend: Price is well below the 200-day SMA with no sign of stabilization
Risk-Return Profile Summary: Nike has historically rewarded patient investors with strong compounding, but the current drawdown is without precedent in 26 years of data. The −68.5% decline from the 2021 peak exceeds anything observed during the dot-com bust, GFC, or COVID crash. Investors should carefully weigh whether this represents a cyclical trough in a durable franchise or a structural de-rating. The 10.6% long-term CAGR demonstrates what Nike can deliver — the question is whether the next decade will resemble the 2010s or the 2020s.

For long-term investors: Nike’s 26-year track record places it among the strongest consumer-brand compounders in the public markets. The current drawdown, while severe, has restored the price to levels that imply ~8x the starting value from 2000 — meaning even after the decline, early investors have earned exceptional returns. The key risk is that the post-2021 decline reflects a permanent competitive shift rather than a temporary setback.

For prospective buyers: Historical precedent within this dataset shows that Nike has never failed to eventually recover from a drawdown and set new highs — but the recovery timeline can span years. Dollar-cost averaging during extended declines has historically been rewarded, though the magnitude of the current drawdown warrants position-sizing discipline.
